passage:
Day one. Over dal, Naveen's mother mentions that Suraj's coaching fees were never paid because the money went to Naveen's master's degree. Naveen says little all evening and lies awake counting the years.

Day four. Naveen still hasn't spoken to Suraj. Calls go to "later." Suraj sends a meme; Naveen leaves it unanswered and feels worse each day. The distance is growing, and Naveen knows it.

Day nine. Naveen drives over and says it plainly: "The money for my degree came from what would have been yours. I should have seen it. I want to make it fair, and I want to hear what fair looks like to you." Suraj is quiet, then says, "Thank you for saying it. Let's work it out slowly." There is no huge gift. They agree to split next year's family costs differently.

qa.q: What did the money for Suraj's coaching fees go to instead?
qa.a: The money went to Naveen's master's degree.

qa.q: Why does Naveen leave Suraj's meme unanswered?
qa.a: Naveen feels guilty and worse each day, and avoiding Suraj feels easier than admitting it, though the distance grows.

qa.q: What did Naveen do on day nine that worked better than silence?
qa.a: Naveen said plainly where the money came from, offered to make it fair, and asked what fair looks like to Suraj instead of handing over a huge gift.

qa.q: How might Suraj have read the days of silence before the visit?
qa.a: Suraj may have felt puzzled or ignored, since a meme went unanswered; the honest visit gave Suraj a reason for the gap and a chance to reply.

grounding: Naveen took more than a fair share of family support, feels guilty, and acknowledges it honestly with a fair repair rather than silence or over-giving.

passage:
The staffroom at the girls' school had emptied for the bell, and Chandrika sat with Gargi's message open on her phone. "Can't make it to Mummy's birthday. Fees for my course are due, working extra shifts."

Chandrika thought of her MBA certificate, framed in her parents' hall. Papa had paid for all of it, and for her wedding. When it was Gargi's turn, the money had run out, and Gargi had taken a loan for a diploma instead. Chandrika had never once said anything about it. It made her stomach twist.

She thought of sending a huge cheque. That would be easy, and it would buy her out of the feeling.

Instead she typed: "Gargi, I got far more support from Mummy-Papa than you did. I've known it for years and never said it. I'm sorry. I'd like to cover this semester's fees, and I'd like to talk properly on Sunday."

The next bell rang. Three dots appeared.

qa.q: Who had paid for Chandrika's MBA and wedding?
qa.a: Papa had paid for all of it.

qa.q: How did Chandrika feel reading Gargi's message?
qa.a: Chandrika felt guilty, her stomach twisting, knowing she had received much more support.

qa.q: Why was Chandrika's message better than a huge cheque?
qa.a: It named the unfairness honestly and offered a fair, specific help plus a real talk, rather than over-giving to erase her guilt.

qa.q: How might Gargi feel reading her sister's message?
qa.a: Gargi might feel surprised and finally seen, since the gap had never been acknowledged before.

grounding: The passage shows a young woman who took more than her share of family support, acknowledging it honestly to her sister and offering fair repair rather than silence or over-giving.

passage:
Dear Shalini,

I'm writing this instead of saying it because I'd lose my nerve.

When Appa got sick, you gave up your hostel seat in Coimbatore to come home and help. I stayed in Chennai and finished my degree. Appa and Amma kept sending me money for the flat, even when there wasn't much. I told myself it was fine. It wasn't.

For years I've felt guilty whenever we talk, and so we've talked less and less. That's the worst of it: my guilt made me distant from the person I owe the most.

I'm sorry. You carried what I didn't.

I'd like to do something fair. I can pay for the evening course you mentioned, and I'll take Appa's hospital visits every other month from now on. I'm not trying to buy back the past. I just want us to be sisters again, the way we were before.

Tell me honestly what you think.

Sudha

qa.q: What did Shalini give up to come home and help?
qa.a: Shalini gave up her hostel seat in Coimbatore.

qa.q: How has guilt affected Sudha over the years?
qa.a: Sudha has felt guilty whenever they talk, which made her pull away and grow distant from her sister.

qa.q: What makes Sudha's offer fair rather than over-giving?
qa.a: It pairs an honest apology with specific, realistic steps, paying for one course and sharing hospital visits, instead of trying to erase the past.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Shalini might feel relieved and respected, since her sacrifice is finally named, even if some hurt remains.

grounding: A letter shows a young woman who took more than her share of family support, feeling guilty, acknowledging it honestly and offering fair, specific repair.
